notable_claims: BBS operators can require users to waive ECPA rights as a condition of use
Waiving ECPA rights may eliminate a sysop's ability to claim protection if their own email is wrongfully seized
Such waivers may prevent users from filing class action suits against the government
classification.summary: The post shares legal advice from Mike Godwin regarding the use of logon disclaimers to waive Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) rights. Godwin argues that such waivers are counterproductive for system operators as they forfeit their own privacy protections and potentially hinder users' ability to pursue class action lawsuits against the government.
classification.title: Logon disclaimers waiving the ECPA

identity.subject: Re: Logon disclaimers waiving the ECPA

notable_claims: Users may waive ECPA protections by continuing to use a system after seeing a disclaimer.
Logon disclaimers that waive ECPA protections eliminate the operator's ability to claim protection if their own email is wrongfully seized.
classification.summary: Mike Godwin of the EFF responds to an inquiry regarding whether BBS logon disclaimers can legally waive protections provided by the Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA). Godwin asserts that while a system operator cannot waive the act, users may effectively do so by continuing to use a system after being notified. He warns that such disclaimers are counterproductive as they strip both operators and users of legal protections against wrongful government seizure of email.
classification.title: Logon disclaimers waiving the ECPA

identity.subject: Re: Logon disclaimers waiving the ECPA

notable_claims: Email monitoring of government employees may impinge on 1st, 4th, and 5th Amendment rights.
Monitoring may violate the Privacy Act and the Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA).
classification.summary: A repost of guidelines from a U.S. government task force regarding the monitoring of government employee emails. The text warns that such monitoring may violate First, Fourth, and Fifth Amendment rights, as well as the Privacy Act and ECPA.
classification.title: Guidelines for government-employee email privacy/monitoring

notable_claims: Email monitoring may impinge on 1st, 4th, and 5th Amendment rights.
Intrusive monitoring can have a 'chilling effect' on system usage.
Agencies should notify employees in advance about the authority, circumstances, and types of monitoring used.
organizations: Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs
classification.summary: This item is an excerpt from a report by the Electronic Mail Task Force prepared for the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). It outlines proposed guidelines for federal agencies regarding the monitoring of employee email, balancing administrative needs with Constitutional rights. The document emphasizes the need for legitimate purposes, least-intrusive methods, and advance notification to employees.
classification.title: Guidelines for government-employee email privacy/monitoring

notable_claims: University rules banning 'porn' on computers are unnecessary and too broad.
classification.summary: This item is a repost of a CAF FAQ arguing against the implementation of university rules that ban pornography on campus computers. The text asserts that such bans are unnecessary and overly broad in scope.
classification.title: Why universities should not create a rule banning computer "porn"

identity.subject: Why universities should not create a rule banning computer "porn"

notable_claims: Banning 'pornography' is too broad because the term is poorly defined and may include fine art.
University computer facilities should be treated like any other university facility by banning harassment rather than materials.
Existing sexual harassment policies are sufficient to handle misconduct without preemptive material bans.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues against university-wide bans on pornography on campus computers, asserting that such rules are overly broad and could inadvertently censor fine art. He suggests that universities should instead enforce existing sexual harassment policies to address the act of harassment rather than banning specific materials. The post includes a curated list of resources from the EFF, AAUP, and ALA regarding academic freedom and obscenity law.
classification.title: Why universities should not create a rule banning computer "porn"
